taxonomic_note: Accepted by current Kew/POWO; broadly native from southeastern Canada through much of the U.S. to Mexico and South America.
look_here_first: Look LOW: nimblewill forms thin, wiry, much-branched stems with short blades often spreading sideways from nodes. Trace one slender SURFACE stolon toward the ground and look for REAL roots coming from its lower nodes; a leaf/stem joint alone is NOT evidence of roots. When flowering, look for an exceptionally NARROW contracted spikelet-bearing panicle (not bermudagrass's fingerlike terminal spikes). Carefully open a fresh blade–sheath junction: nimblewill has a minute membranous, often uneven/ciliolate ligule; bermudagrass has a fringe of hairs instead. If rooting, ligule and seedhead are hidden, leave at Muhlenbergia sp. until confirmed.

project_inclusion.range_basis: USDA-derived Texas county/native-status data list native occurrences in Hays, Travis and Williamson Counties, among many others. UT Plant Resources Center's Selected Central Texas Grasses includes M. schreberi for the NW Hays/Travis-centered regional flora.
project_inclusion.range_guardrail: County decision uses USDA-derived native county data; lawn/yard occurrence is not treated as native evidence by itself.

best_field_traits: weak perennial grass with decumbent much-branched culms
lower stem nodes root and allow patches to spread
usually only 10–40 cm tall, occasionally taller
leaf blades short and flat, roughly 2–8 cm long and 1–4 mm wide
ligule minute, a short membrane/ciliolate membrane
panicle narrow and contracted, about 5–15 cm
panicle branches short and appressed to ascending
morphology_keys.comparison_training: Muhlenbergia lindheimeri: Lindheimer muhly is a large upright fountain-form bunchgrass with long basal leaves and a huge feathery panicle. Muhlenbergia reverchonii: Seep muhly is a compact upright tuft with threadlike leaves and open airy panicle; nimblewill creeps and roots at nodes. Cynodon dactylon: Bermudagrass also creeps but has digitate fingerlike seedheads and obvious stolon/rhizome architecture unlike the narrow Muhlenbergia panicle.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: Whole creeping patch showing distinct horizontal stems and short side-pointing leaves.
Stem tracked to the SOIL to show a node actually issuing roots (not merely a leaf insertion).
Macro of blade/sheath junction and short membranous ligule at 10–20×.
Mature narrow panicle, a separate single-flowered awned spikelet at millimeter scale.
Same-scale Cynodon dactylon spike versus Muhlenbergia schreberi panicle.
crew_field_check: Start at the soil. Follow the thin stems sideways: their leaf blades come off at many joints rather than one fountainlike basal crown.
Find a distinct stem node with attached blade/sheath; a root emerging here would confirm the creeping-rooting growth form, but today's pictures do not prove root emergence.
Compare the short-leaved stems and narrow seedhead to Cynodon: bermudagrass has fingerlike terminal racemes and a hair-fringe ligule.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Nimblewill (M. schreberi) has slender above-ground stolons capable of ROOTING AT THE NODES, short sideways leaves, and narrow contracted terminal/axillary panicles. Bermudagrass (Cynodon dactylon) also has stolons, but produces several fingerlike racemes from a common tip and a HAIR FRINGE in place of the membranous ligule. Aparejo muhly (M. utilis) instead possesses BELOW-GROUND scaly RHIZOMES, very thin often rolled blades and tiny narrow heads; current appearjo photos DO NOT expose its rhizomes. Creeping bentgrass has a membranous but usually much longer ligule and a different open flowering structure. Kew describes a ciliate-edged membrane about 1 mm for nimblewill while regional flora/Ohio State descriptions include 0.1–0.5 mm: do not use one hard millimeter cutoff. Compare multiple characters. Preserve native-range checks as originally recorded.

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Nimblewill — look here first
steps: Begin with current real nimblewill image 1: point out short leaf blades and actual LEAF/STEM attachment points on upright wiry branches. These are not yet photographed as rooted.
Use the second local photo to show narrow short blades and leaf sheath shape; no ligule is sufficiently resolved to label in either current photo.
Follow a stem to soil; photograph an above-ground stolon and one visibly ROOTED node in one connected frame with a millimeter scale. If the node merely touches soil, the roots are NOT verified.
Open an attached fresh leaf at the blade/sheath junction; under a hand lens find a short MEMBRANOUS/ciliolate ligule, not the longer obvious fringe of hairs typical of bermudagrass.
Photograph the very narrow contracted flowering panicle, preferably with a hand or mm scale and one mature spikelet. Bermudagrass has several fingerlike racemes from one tip; nimblewill does not.
Compare appeared-as-other-species M. utilis: only the fine foliage is pictured, never its underground scaly rhizomes. Investigate suspected plants carefully before assigning species.
field_photo_quickcheck.field_rule: Use the photographed growth-form details only to choose a candidate. Confirm with the missing rooting/rhizome/ligule reproductive details.
field_photo_quickcheck.warning: No current local-photo arrows establish root-emitting nodes, a true opened membranous ligule, or a mature measured spikelet. Botanical references support those diagnostic characters but source citations DO NOT replace photographs. Current University extension rooting-node illustration is a COPYRIGHTED external study image, not imported absent reuse authorization. Future Emily Summerbell CC BY Commons close-ups must remain photo-ID attributed and inspected from saved bytes before being promoted.

field_id_finish_pass.crew_teaching_summary: Look LOW, not for an ornamental bunch: nimblewill makes thin branching stems that creep across the ground with short, nearly horizontal blades. It can root from the lower stem nodes. Inspect a real node and then find a slender narrow panicle, often spike-like because its branches hug the axis. Confirm the short membranous/ciliolate ligule; do not identify a grass from the creeping habit alone.
